title: Scoping a project when the idea is still loose
metaTitle: Scoping when the idea is still loose
excerpt: When the idea is loose, name what you do not know and scope a first slice that will teach the rest. A scope that pretends the whole product is clear will slip.
primaryKeyword: how to scope a website project
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops. The notes are the right size for a loose idea: visible unknowns, not a finished map.
caption: Name the unknown before you price the whole thing. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is a first slice when the idea is loose?
faqs.answer: A first slice is the smallest public or usable version that tests the offer. For a site, that might be a homepage and a way to talk to you. For a product, it is one workflow, including the empty state and the error. The slice is real work, chosen because finishing it will teach the next scope.

faqs.question: Should a loose idea be priced as the full product?
faqs.answer: Price the slice you can describe, and write down what is still unknown. A fixed price on an undescribed product becomes a dispute. A range is fair when the unknowns are named, and the next price comes after the slice has answered them.

faqs.question: What should the scope document say about changes?
faqs.answer: Say what a change does to the date. A new page, a new audience, or a new account type is a change to the slice, not a note in the margin. Either it replaces something already in the slice, or the date moves. Write that rule before the work starts.

markdown:
How to scope a website project when the idea is still loose: name the unknown, then scope a first slice that will teach the rest. Do not write a document that pretends the whole product is already clear.

A loose idea is a normal starting point. Founders often have a name, a dissatisfaction with the current site, and a sense of the customer. They do not yet have a page list, a catalog model, or the one action the site should earn. A scope that invents those in order to look complete will be renegotiated in week two. A scope that labels them as unknown can be priced and started.

## Name the unknown

Write the gaps as sentences, not as a vibe. Each one should be something a slice could answer.

- Who the first version is for, if two audiences are still fighting.
- The one action you want: a call, an order, a signup, a download.
- What already exists and must survive: a URL, a product name, a checkout, a login.
- What you hope is true and have not checked: that people will understand the offer in a sentence, that the catalog is this many products, that the team can edit the site.

Unknowns are not failures. They are the brief. A studio can estimate a slice beside a list like that. It cannot honestly estimate “the platform” beside a blank.

Separate taste from the gap. “I do not like the current colors” is a preference. “A stranger cannot tell what we sell” is an unknown the first page has to close. Google’s guidance on [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a clean test for that second kind: the page should satisfy the person who arrived, and it should be written for them. If you cannot yet say who that person is, the scope’s first job is to pick a working answer and try it, not to design twelve pages for a crowd you have not chosen.

## The first slice

The slice is the smallest thing you would be willing to show. It has an edge.

For a company site, a homepage that says what you do and how to talk to you is often enough to learn from. Add one supporting page if a second question is already blocking sales: the product, the service, or proof. Leave the blog, the careers page, and the interactive tour until someone asks for them with a real reason.

For a shop, the slice might be a dozen products, one product template, and a checkout you can run in test. The rest of the catalog can wait until the template is right. Migrating every plugin on day one teaches you nothing except how the old theme behaved.

For a product interface, the slice is one workflow a user finishes: empty, success, and failure. A wide app with rough edges everywhere is not a slice. It is the loose idea drawn in full.

Hanabi’s projects work this way when the idea arrives unfinished. The studio would rather ship a clear page, in a repository you own, than storyboard a product nobody has agreed on. The stack stays ordinary: Figma for the options, then Next.js and React once the slice is real enough to build.

## What the slice must include

A thin slice still has to be finished. Finished means a stranger can complete the job without you in the room.

Include the words. A page of boxes labeled “headline” is not a slice you can learn from. Write the sentence you are willing to say, even if you expect to revise it. The revision is the lesson.

Include the primary action and the place it goes: a calendar, an email, a cart. An action that lands nowhere teaches you that the button was decorative.

Include the state people actually hit. A shop slice includes a sold-out variant or it has not met the catalog. A product slice includes the first empty screen or it has only met the demo. A marketing slice includes the mobile width, because that is where many founders will check it, and where a desktop composition often falls apart.

Include what you will own at the end of the slice: the repo, the domain plan, the content fields. A slice that lives only in a design file has not tested the build. If the unknown was “can we edit this,” the slice has to answer with a field, not a promise.

Leave a written non-goal. “Not in this slice: accounts, a second language, the investor page.” Non-goals keep helpful ideas from becoming silent scope. They also give the next slice a place to start.

## What a change does to the date

Loose ideas keep producing new thoughts. That is useful, and it is how dates die if every thought joins the slice.

Agree on a rule before the work starts. A change that adds an audience, a page, or a flow either replaces something in the slice or moves the date. It does not hide inside “quick.” Quick is how a homepage becomes a platform between critiques.

The person who can approve should be the person who accepts the trade. Feedback from a teammate is welcome. A new requirement from someone who does not hold the date is how the slice swells. Capture it on a list for the next slice. Read that list at the end. You will often find the second slice sitting there, already named.

If the change reveals that the slice was the wrong slice, stop and re-scope. That is cheaper than finishing a polished answer to the wrong question. A studio should say so. Flexibility is a process that can change, not a willingness to absorb every addition for free.

## When the rest becomes clear

Review the slice against the unknowns you wrote down. Which ones did it answer? Which ones are still open because you have now seen a real page?

Typical answers after a first site slice: the sentence is wrong and needs a rewrite, the proof is thinner than you thought, the action people click is not the one you emphasized. Those are successful findings. The next scope is specific because of them.

Typical answers after a product slice: the workflow is right and the adjacent settings can wait, or the workflow was a founder habit and the next user needs a different start. Either way you know more than you did when the idea was a paragraph.

Only then price the rest. The rest might be more pages, a catalog, or a decision to stop. Stopping is allowed. A slice that shows the offer is not ready is a cheap lesson compared with a six-month build of the same doubt.

When the idea is no longer loose, and you are scoping a marketing site from pages and states, the method changes. That piece is [how a marketing site gets scoped so the date survives](/blog/scoping-a-marketing-site).

If you want help naming the slice before anyone pretends the whole product is known, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the unknowns. The call should leave you with a first edge, not a map of everything.
